column3: The smallest constellation, a kite-shaped cross of four bright stars in the Milky Way.
column4: High in the south on autumn and winter evenings (April to July); low in the south-east or south-west at other times.
column5: Look for the two bright Pointers; they point straight at the cross. A fainter fifth star sits off-centre.
column6: Tswana and Sotho see the Pointers and two brightest Cross stars as four giraffes; the /Xam saw lionesses.
column7: Extend the long axis of the cross 4.5 times to find celestial south, then drop straight down to the horizon.

column3: The great hunter, one of the brightest constellations, with red Betelgeuse and blue-white Rigel.
column4: Summer evenings (December to March), high in the north; from Botswana the hunter appears upside down.
column5: Find the three equal stars in a short straight row (the Belt); the four bright stars around them form the body.
column6: Greek myth: Apollo sent a scorpion to sting Orion, so Orion sets in the west as Scorpius rises in the east.
column7: Orion and Scorpius are never seen high in the sky together; they sit on opposite sides of the sky.

column3: An asterism: three bright stars in a neat row that form the belt of Orion.
column4: Summer evenings (December to March), rising in the east after sunset and later high in the north.
column5: Three equal, bright stars in a short straight line; follow the line one way to Sirius.
column6: Tswana and Sotho call these stars Dikolobe, the three pigs; Khoikhoi saw three zebras.
column7: Follow the Belt one way to brilliant Sirius and the other way to orange Aldebaran.

column3: The Great Dog constellation, home of Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
column4: Summer evenings (December to April), high overhead, just east of Orion.
column5: Follow Orion's Belt east (away from Aldebaran) to the very bright star Sirius, the dog's nose.
column6: In Greek stories it is one of Orion's hunting dogs following its master across the sky.
column7: Sirius is only about 8.6 light years away, one of the closest stars to us.

column3: The scorpion, a large hook-shaped constellation with the red giant Antares as its heart.
column4: Winter evenings (May to September); in mid-winter it is almost overhead in the early evening.
column5: Look for a long curved line of stars like a fish-hook, with bright red Antares near the top.
column6: Greek myth: the gods sent the scorpion to sting Orion; now Scorpius rises as Orion sets.
column7: Astronomical Scorpius is not the same as astrological Scorpio, which today falls in Libra.

column3: The keel of a ship, home of Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky.
column4: Best on summer and autumn evenings (January to May), in the south and south-west.
column5: Find Canopus, the bright star far south of Sirius; the rest of Carina runs towards the Southern Cross.
column6: Once part of a giant ship constellation, Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts.
column7: Carina holds the Carina Nebula and the False Cross, which guests often confuse with the real Southern Cross.

column3: The bull, with orange Aldebaran as the bull's eye and the Pleiades on its shoulder.
column4: Summer evenings (December to February), low in the north, to the left of Orion as you face north.
column5: Follow Orion's Belt away from Sirius to a V-shape of stars (the Hyades) with orange Aldebaran.
column6: In Greek myth Zeus turned himself into a white bull to carry off Princess Europa.
column7: Taurus is one of the 12 zodiac constellations, so planets and the Moon pass through it.

column3: The lion, a zodiac constellation with the bright star Regulus.
column4: Autumn evenings (March to May), in the north.
column5: Look for a backwards question mark of stars (the Sickle) ending in bright Regulus, the lion's heart.
column6: Greek myth: the Nemean lion, killed by Hercules as the first of his twelve labours.
column7: A good one for a lion-loving safari crowd; the Leonid meteor shower comes from this area in November.

column3: Two bright stars of Centaurus, Alpha and Beta Centauri, that point to the Southern Cross.
column4: Autumn and winter evenings (April to August), high in the south, beside the Southern Cross.
column5: Find the two brightest stars near the Cross; a line from them points at the cross.
column6: Tswana and Sotho saw them as two giraffes; the /Xam (San) saw two male lions.
column7: They look like twins but are not: Alpha is about 4.3 light years away, Beta is over 300 light years away.

column3: The nearest star system to the Sun: three stars, Alpha Centauri A and B and faint Proxima Centauri.
column4: Autumn and winter evenings, high in the south; it is the brighter of the two Pointers.
column5: Find the Southern Cross, then the brighter Pointer, the one further from the Cross.
column6: One of the four giraffes (Tswana and Sotho) or one of the two male lions (/Xam).
column7: Light from Alpha Centauri takes over 4 years to reach us; Proxima is the closest star to Earth after the Sun.

column3: The brightest star in the night sky, a white star with a tiny white dwarf companion.
column4: Summer evenings (December to April), high in the east and later almost overhead.
column5: Follow Orion's Belt to the south-east to the brightest, twinkling star in the sky.
column6: Ancient Egyptians used the first dawn rising of Sirius to predict the yearly Nile flood.
column7: Sirius often flashes many colours when it is low, because our air bends and splits its light.

column3: The second-brightest star in the night sky, a white giant in the constellation Carina.
column4: Summer evenings high in the south (January to April); in winter it rises before dawn in the south-east.
column5: Look far to the south of Sirius for a second, almost as bright, white star.
column6: Sotho and Tswana call Canopus Naka (the horn); its dawn rising in winter was a sign of the new season.
column7: Canopus is much further away than Sirius (over 300 light years) but gives out thousands of times more light.

column3: A huge red supergiant star in Orion; if it replaced our Sun it would swallow Mars.
column4: Summer evenings (December to March) in the north; the orange-red star in Orion.
column5: Find Orion's Belt; Betelgeuse is the bright orange-red star on one side of it, opposite blue Rigel.
column6: In a Khoikhoi story Betelgeuse is a lion watching the three zebras of the Belt.
column7: Betelgeuse is near the end of its life and will one day explode as a supernova.

column3: A very bright blue-white supergiant star in Orion, many thousands of times brighter than the Sun.
column4: Summer evenings (December to March); in Orion, high in the north.
column5: Find Orion's Belt; Rigel is the bright blue-white star on the opposite side from red Betelgeuse.
column7: Compare Rigel and Betelgeuse with guests: star colour shows temperature, blue is hot and red is cooler.

column3: A red supergiant star, the bright red heart of Scorpius.
column4: Winter evenings (May to September), almost overhead in mid-winter.
column5: Find the hook-shaped Scorpius; Antares is the bright red star in the body of the scorpion.
column6: Its name means "rival of Mars" because its red colour looks like the planet Mars.
column7: Antares is so big that it would reach past the orbit of Mars if it sat where our Sun is.

column3: An orange giant star, the bright eye of Taurus the bull.
column4: Summer evenings (December to February), low in the north.
column5: Follow Orion's Belt away from Sirius to a bright orange star at the tip of a V of stars.
column6: In a Khoikhoi story Aldebaran is the hunter whose arrow (Orion's sword) fell short of the three zebras.
column7: Aldebaran is not part of the V-shaped Hyades cluster; it lies about half as far away.

column3: A bright white star in Canis Minor, the Little Dog, with a white dwarf companion.
column4: Summer evenings (December to April), in the north-east, east of Orion.
column5: Make a triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse; Procyon is the bright star at the third corner.
column7: Its name means "before the dog" because it rises just before Sirius, the Dog Star, in northern lands.

column3: The North Star, which sits almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole.
column4: Not visible from Botswana: it is always below our northern horizon; guests from the north know it well.
column5: In the northern hemisphere, draw a line from Polaris straight down to the horizon to find true north.
column7: The south has no bright pole star, which is why we use the Southern Cross and Pointers to find south.

column3: Our own star, about 70% hydrogen and 28% helium, at the centre of the solar system.
column4: Never look at the Sun directly or through binoculars; it can blind you.
column7: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross the 150 million km to Earth.

column3: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, a rocky world covered in craters.
column4: Only low in the west just after sunset or low in the east just before sunrise, for a few weeks at a time.
column5: Look low near the horizon in bright twilight for a steady, star-like dot that does not twinkle.
column6: Named after the fast messenger of the Roman gods, because it moves quickly around the Sun.
column7: Mercury goes around the Sun in only 88 days.

column3: The brightest planet, about the size of Earth, wrapped in thick white clouds.
column4: Only in the west after sunset (evening star) or in the east before sunrise (morning star).
column5: The brightest point of light in the sky after the Moon; it shines steadily and does not twinkle.
column6: Named after the Roman goddess of love; many cultures thought the evening and morning stars were different objects.
column7: Venus is so bright it can cast a shadow on a dark night, far from lights.

column3: The red planet, a small rocky world with iron-rich red dust.
column4: Varies year to year; it moves along the zodiac line, and is brightest about every 26 months.
column5: Look along the zodiac line for a steady orange-red point that does not twinkle.
column6: Named after the Roman god of war because of its blood-red colour.
column7: Mars has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about three times as high as Everest.

column3: The largest planet, a gas giant more than 11 times wider than Earth.
column4: Moves slowly along the zodiac line; it can be seen through the whole night when well placed.
column5: Very bright and steady; binoculars show up to four tiny moons (the Galilean moons) in a line.
column6: Named after the king of the Roman gods.
column7: Jupiter's four big moons were discovered by Galileo in 1610 and can be seen with binoculars.

column3: A gas giant planet with beautiful bright rings of ice and rock.
column4: Moves slowly along the zodiac line; it stays in roughly the same constellation for about two years.
column5: A steady, creamy-yellow point on the zodiac line; a small telescope shows the rings.
column6: Named after the Roman god of farming and time.
column7: Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a big enough bath of water.

column3: The Moon fully lit by the Sun, when the Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon.
column4: Rises in the east at sunset and sets in the west at sunrise.
column5: A full moon makes the sky bright, so stars and the Milky Way are hard to see.
column6: Some San believed eclipses happened when a lion covered the full moon with its paw so it could hunt.
column7: Only at full moon can a lunar eclipse happen.

column3: A thin, less-than-half lit Moon; seen after new moon (waxing) or before new moon (waning).
column4: A waxing crescent is in the west after sunset; a waning crescent is in the east before sunrise.
column5: Look low in the west just after sunset a few days after new moon.
column6: Some San said the Sun's sharp rays cut pieces off the Moon-man until he begged for mercy and grew again.
column7: The faint glow on the dark part is earthshine: sunlight reflected from Earth onto the Moon.

column3: A more-than-half lit Moon, between first quarter and full moon or between full and third quarter.
column4: A waxing gibbous moon is high in the east in the early evening.
column5: Waxing means growing (new to full); waning means shrinking (full to new).
column7: Along the line between light and dark, binoculars show craters and mountains in sharp shadow.

column3: Our home galaxy, a spiral of up to 400 billion stars, about 100 000 light years across.
column4: Best on dark, moonless winter evenings (June to August), stretching overhead through Scorpius.
column5: Look for the band of misty light across a dark sky; it is brightest towards Scorpius and Sagittarius.
column6: San say a girl threw wood ashes into the sky to light the way home; Tswana call it Molalatladi.
column7: The band is our flat galaxy seen edge-on from inside; we see more stars when we look along the disc.

column3: A small galaxy close to our own, about 160 000 light years away.
column4: Best on summer evenings (November to March), high in the south.
column5: Looks like a detached piece of the Milky Way; find it about halfway between Canopus and the south pole.
column6: Named after the explorer Magellan, whose crew described the clouds on their voyage around the world.
column7: One of only three galaxies (besides our own) that you can see with the naked eye.

column3: A small galaxy close to our own, about 200 000 light years away.
column4: Best on spring and summer evenings (October to February), high in the south.
column5: A smaller misty patch than the Large Cloud, near the bright star Achernar.
column6: Named after the explorer Magellan, whose crew described the clouds on their voyage around the world.
column7: Light from the Small Cloud left it about 200 000 years ago, when modern humans first appeared in Africa.

column3: A giant spiral galaxy, the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way.
column4: Low in the north on spring evenings (October to December); needs a very dark sky.
column5: A faint oval smudge low in the north; easier to find with binoculars.
column6: Named after the princess Andromeda of Greek myth.
column7: At about 2.5 million light years, it is the most distant object most people can see with the naked eye.

column3: A cluster of young, hot blue stars, the Seven Sisters, in Taurus.
column4: Summer evenings (November to February), low in the north; it disappears for a few weeks in May.
column5: Follow Orion's Belt past Aldebaran to a small, tight group of stars like a tiny dipper.
column6: Xhosa and Zulu call it Isilimela, Tswana Selemela; its return before dawn in June is the sign to plough.
column7: Most people see six or seven stars; binoculars show dozens.

column3: A dark cloud of dust that blocks the light of the stars behind it.
column4: Autumn and winter evenings (April to July), beside the Southern Cross.
column5: Look for the dark hole in the Milky Way just next to the bottom-left of the Southern Cross.
column6: Aboriginal Australians see it as the head of a great Emu in the sky, whose body is dark dust lanes.
column7: It is about 600 light years away and contains material for new stars.

column3: A small, bright cluster of young stars in the Southern Cross.
column4: Autumn and winter evenings (April to July), in the Southern Cross.
column5: Look just next to Beta Crux (the left-hand star of the Cross); binoculars show a fuzzy little group.
column6: John Herschel, observing from the Cape in the 1830s, compared it to a box of coloured jewels.
column7: Through a telescope one orange star stands out among the blue-white ones.

column3: The biggest globular cluster of the Milky Way, a ball of about 10 million old stars.
column4: Autumn and winter evenings (April to July), high in the south-east to south.
column5: From the Southern Cross go up towards Centaurus; it looks like a fuzzy star to the naked eye.
column7: Early astronomers thought it was a single star, which is why it has a star name.

column3: A huge glowing cloud of gas where new stars are being born, about 1 300 light years away.
column4: Summer evenings (December to March), in Orion.
column5: Just next to Orion's Belt is a short line of stars (the sword); the middle 'star' is a misty patch.
column7: It is the brightest star nursery in the sky and easy to see in binoculars.

column3: The Earth's shadow covers the full moon, turning it a dull reddish-brown.
column4: Only at full moon; can be seen from anywhere on Earth where the Moon is up.
column5: Safe to watch with naked eyes or binoculars; check eclipse dates in advance.
column6: Some San believed a lion put his paw over the full moon because it was too light to hunt.
column7: Lunar eclipses are much more common to see than solar eclipses.

column3: The Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the Sun.
column4: Only at new moon, and only in a narrow path on Earth; rare at any one place.
column5: Never look at the Sun with naked eyes, binoculars or a telescope; use proper eclipse glasses.
column7: In a total eclipse the Sun's glowing outer atmosphere, the corona, becomes visible.

column3: A streak of light made when a small space rock (meteoroid) burns up in our air.
column4: Any clear, dark night; more are seen after midnight.
column5: Lie back, let your eyes adjust to the dark for 20 minutes and watch a wide area of sky.
column7: Most shooting stars come from grains no bigger than a grain of sand.

column3: Many meteors in one night, when Earth passes through dust left behind by a comet.
column4: Fixed dates each year; the manual names the Perseids (mid-August), Geminids (mid-December) are good from Botswana.
column5: The meteors seem to come from one point in the sky, which gives the shower its name.
column7: The Perseids sit low in the north from Botswana, so northern-hemisphere guests see more of them at home.

column3: A space rock that survives its fall through the air and lands on Earth.
column7: The world's largest known meteorite, Hoba (about 60 tonnes), lies in Namibia.
